p01.why: The size of a closure is unspecified, but every class has size at least 1 and a copy capture of an int holds an int member, so both checks hold on every layout I can think of.

p02.why: The array is copied element by element and r copies the int it refers to, so later changes are not seen and the call gives 2 * 10 + 3 = 23.

p03.why: A lambda with a capture does not convert to a pointer to function.

p04.why: Both the outer and the inner lambda capture a, so the inner one returns 1.

p05.why: The copy b = a is fine, but a closure with captures cannot be assigned.

p06.why: The mutable closure changes its own copy, so the second call gives 2 and the outer n stays 0.

p07.why: A closure type with captures cannot be default-constructed.

p08.why: A generic lambda without captures converts to any pointer type that deduction can match, and the constexpr call through next is a constant expression.

p09.why: A closure without captures can be default-constructed and assigned.

p10.why: [=] captures this implicitly, the compilers warn that this is deprecated, and -Werror turns the warning into an error; the specification only says implementations should warn, so this rests on outside knowledge.

p11.why: A reference capture can be changed without mutable, so x becomes 5.

p12.why: Reference captures see the later change to 5 and make the change to 9.

p13.why: Lambdas can appear in decltype and sizeof, and the two lambda expressions have different types.

p14.why: A namespace-scope lambda can have an init capture, and the mutable call increments it from 3 to 4.

p15.why: A static lambda must not capture anything.

p16.why: Each lambda expression has its own closure type.

p17.why: [&, this], [=, this], and [=, *this] are the listed exceptions to the same-mode rule.

p18.why: A variable of abstract class type cannot be captured by copy.

p19.why: The explicit capture a uses copy, the same mode as the default =.

p20.why: [this] changes c.n to 1, and [*this] increments its own copy to 2 while c.n stays 1.

p21.why: The call operators are constexpr when the body permits, and a lambda can be called where it is created.

p22.why: The inner lambda captures a, but the enclosing lambda does not capture a.

p23.why: GCC 16 and EDG find the capture, so the return type is const int& and the assertion holds; Clang and GCC 14 find the outer x, give int&, and then reject the return of the const capture (Q-0092).

p24.why: A lambda can have a default argument and its call operator is constexpr.

p25.why: A noexcept lambda without captures converts to a pointer to a noexcept function.

p26.why: The body takes the address of the local constant c without capturing it.

p27.why: The closure calls through a reference to inner after inner has ended, which is undefined; with AddressSanitizer at -O0 I expect a use-after-scope report and a nonzero exit, which is outside knowledge.

p28.why: A lambda must not be mutable and also have an explicit object parameter.

p29.why: The body only reads the value of the constant c, so no capture is needed.

p30.why: A data member cannot be captured by its name.

p31.why: The lambda is called where it is created and returns 6.

p32.why: The explicit object parameter lets the lambda call itself, and the call is constexpr, giving 120.

p33.why: An auto parameter deduces int and double, and the return type follows.

p34.why: f is not a member function, so the lambda cannot capture this.

p35.why: Init captures are initialized in list order, so mark(1) runs before mark(2).

p36.why: Explicit copy captures and init captures are initialized in list order, giving 3, 1, 2 and then 2, 7, 1.

p37.why: The copy capture keeps the value 1 from when the lambda was evaluated.

p38.why: The returned closure reads local after local has ended, which is undefined, and constant evaluation must reject undefined behavior.

p39.why: &a uses the same mode as the default &.

p40.why: Captureless lambdas convert to function pointers, by initialization and by unary +.

p41.why: A parameter has the name of an explicit capture.

p42.why: The body uses the local a without capturing it.

p43.why: A lambda in a default argument must not capture anything.

p44.why: global has static storage, and only automatic variables can be captured.

p45.why: The name a occurs twice in the capture list.

p46.why: A lambda in a default member initializer can capture this, and v is initialized before got and all.

p47.why: The initializer x * 10 looks up the outer x, so the capture holds 20.

p48.why: A reference init capture bound to a temporary through a static_cast to a reference extends the temporary to the life of the closure.

p49.why: Structured bindings can be captured, by copy and by reference.

p50.why: The body changes a copy capture without mutable.

p51.why: The returns give int and double with no trailing return type.

p52.why: x holds 6 and r aliases v, so v becomes 4.

p53.why: Both constants are only read as values, so they need no capture.

p54.why: The generic body is a templated context, so the dependent call probe(item) is looked up at instantiation and finds lib::probe by argument-dependent lookup.

p55.why: The deduced and trailing return types are int and long, and the call b(3) is constexpr.

p56.why: Each of a, b, and x is initialized once in some order, and the call gives 10.

p57.why: c copied a and b before r changes a to 10.

p58.why: g copies a and refers to b, so b becomes 1; h copies a and refers to b, so h gives 2.

p59.why: The body uses the member v without capturing this.

p60.why: A static lambda has a static call operator, the call is constexpr, and the closure converts to a pointer to function.

p61.why: A namespace-scope lambda has a capture default; Clang and GCC reject and EDG accepts (Q-0037).

p62.why: Globals and local statics need no capture.
